newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Troops ease grip on Armenian capital.
newsitem.headline: Troops ease grip on Armenian capital.

text.p: Troops eased their grip on the Armenian capital of Yerevan on Saturday, two days after being sent into the streets by President Levon Ter-Petrosyan to counter a mass protest against his re-election.
Some of the thousands of troops quit the city centre altogether while others unblocked main avenues, letting public transport run freely.
Ten light tanks and scores of camouflage-clad conscripts were still concentrated in the middle of the vast Respublika square, the city's focal point.

A ban on demonstrations and public gatherings was still in force but pedestrians resumed the habit of strolling or sitting near the large fountain in the square that had been deserted since the troops were sent in on Thursday.

Ter-Petrosyan turned to the army after a violent clash between demonstrators and riot police on Wednesday. A presidential aide said on Thursday two people were killed and dozens injured, but deputy health minister Derenik Dumanyan on Saturday denied that anyone had died.

Supporters of opposition leader Vazgen Manukyan were protesting what Manukyan alleged was the rigging of the presidential vote on September 22. Preliminary results give Ter-Petrosyan 52 percent of the vote to 41 percent for Manukyan, a former prime minister.
Final results, due to be issued on Sunday, are not expected to differ substantially.

Some demonstrators tore down a fence around parliament, entered the building and assaulted its speaker and his deputy. They were dispersed when police and troops opened fire over their heads, sprayed water cannon and used tear gas.

The aloof 51-year old President says the melee was an attempted "fascist" coup by "mentally ill people". As well as dispatching troops, he closed the headquarters of some opposition parties who have claimed dozens of their members have been rounded up by security organs.

Parir Hayrikyan, a member of Manukyan's broad opposition coalition, said the 50-year old physicist incited protesters by telling them to "come after him" if he did not return within 30 minutes from the parliament, where he was negotiating with the head of the Central Electoral Commission.

"This was a miscalculation, and it was morally wrong. He was under pressure by some of his associates who were not satisfied just going to the parliament to cry. It was a big mistake," said Hayrikyan, a former Soviet-era dissident who spent 17 years in labour camps.

But he scoffed at Ter-Petrosyan's allegations it was a coup. "This is blasphemous. How can unarmed people stage a coup? The President and his circle are using this now to terrorise the population. They are punishing people because they didn't vote for Ter-Petrosyan," he said.
Hayrikyan claimed that about 100 opposition activists had been arrested in three days and that some had been beaten "half to death" by the security forces.

Ter-Petrosyan aide Jerair Liparityan has said details of arrests will be issued later. He defended using the army to quell the unrest, saying that if something similar had happened in the United States, the protesters would have been shot.

Manukyan, who has gone into hiding, can be arrested for allegedly inspiring the unrest after he loses special candidate immunity from prosecution. That will happen when final official results are published.
Ter-Petrosyan won only two percent more than the 50 percent required to claim a second five-year term and avoid a runoff with Manukyan.
International observers reported instances of fraud and irregularities, the overwhelming majority of which they said were committed by the President's supporters.

Many observers have said they believe opposition charges that the abuses were responsible for putting Ter-Petrosyan over the 50 percent threshold. They say he would have at least faced a second round against Manukyan.

"It's very difficult to quantify but when the margin is only one or two percent, I think the irregularities we saw certainly could have impacted on the result," said one foreign monitor who did not want to be identified.
